title: A meeting at the Cirque Moderne
why: Reed dates it only to the weeks before the rising; the meetings were held at night.
sum: Across the river, in the bare amphitheatre of the Cirque Moderne, soldiers, sailors and workers pack the benches to hear a soldier from the front.
q: I went across the river to the Cirque Moderne, to one of the great popular meetings which occurred all over the city, more numerous night after night.

also.q: The bare, gloomy amphitheatre, lit by five tiny lights hanging from a thin wire, was packed from the ring up the steep sweep of grimy benches

ref.q: The bare, gloomy amphitheatre, lit by five tiny lights hanging from a thin wire, was packed from the ring up the steep sweep of grimy benches

title: Ten thousand at the Obukhov works
why: “One Sunday” in October; 28 Oct is a guess within the range, chosen only to order the scenes.
sum: One Sunday Reed rides a steam tram out along the Schlüsselburg Prospekt to a meeting of ten thousand at the Obukhov munitions plant; Lunatcharsky speaks.
q: ten thousand black-clothed men and women packed around a scaffolding draped in red, people heaped on piles of lumber and bricks, perched high upon shadowy girders

also.q: One Sunday we went, on a top-heavy steam tram that lumbered through oceans of mud, between stark factories and immense churches

present.size: ten thousand black-clothed men and women

title: Out to Smolny by streetcar
why: Undated; placed before the night session of 30 Oct only to order the scenes.
sum: Reed rides a crawling, jammed streetcar to the end of the line at Smolny, the Soviets’ headquarters “miles out on the edge of the city”.
q: Smolny Institute, headquarters of the Tsay-ee-kah and of the Petrograd Soviet, lay miles out on the edge of the city, beside the wide Neva.

also.q: I went there on a street-car, moving snail-like with a groaning noise through the cobbled, muddy streets, and jammed with people.

title: Trotzky denies an insurrection
why: “The night of October 30th”, New Style.
sum: At the Petrograd Soviet’s stormy all-night meeting, at which Reed is present, Trotzky calls the press’s talk of an armed rising an attempt “to discredit and wreck the Congress of Soviets”.
q: At a meeting of the Petrograd Soviet in Smolny, the night of October 30th, Trotzky branded the assertions of the bourgeois press

also.q: Stormy was the all-night meeting of the Petrograd Soviet the 30th of October, at which I was present.

title: The Day of the Petrograd Soviet
sum: Sunday 4 Nov is the Day of the Petrograd Soviet, with mass meetings all over the city; the Cossacks’ rival procession is called off.
q: Sunday, November 4th, was designated as the Day of the Petrograd Soviet, with immense meetings planned all over the city

title: The Council of the Republic
sum: Reed drops in on the Council of the Russian Republic, in bitter debate on Terestchenko’s foreign policy.
q: Monday morning, the 5th, I dropped in at the Marinsky Palace, to see what was happening in the Council of the Russian Republic.

title: Yunkers on the Morskaya
sum: Outside, two companies of yunkers march up the Morskaya singing; at the corner of the Nevsky Reed buys Lenin’s pamphlet. Up the Nevsky crowds battle for the latest papers, soldiers and students argue on the corners, and an armoured car goes slowly up and down.
q: Two companies of yunkers passed swinging up the Morskaya
At the corner of the Nevsky I bought a pamphlet by Lenin

also.q: Up the Nevsky in the sour twilight crowds were battling for the latest papers
An armoured automobile went slowly up and down, siren screaming.

ref.q: Two companies of yunkers passed swinging up the Morskaya, tramping stiffly in their long coats and singing an oldtime crashing chorus, such as the soldiers used to sing under the Tsar
An armoured automobile went slowly up and down, siren screaming.
Up the Nevsky in the sour twilight crowds were battling for the latest papers
On every corner, in every open space, thick groups were clustered; arguing soldiers and students.

title: A film by the Kazan Cathedral
why: After the twilight walk up the Nevsky and before Smolny, where Reed stays until three.
sum: Reed watches a bloody Italian film near the Kazan Cathedral; soldiers and sailors in front stare in wonder.
q: We went to a moving picture show near the Kazan Cathedral—a bloody Italian film of passion and intrigue.

ref.q: Night came swiftly down, the wide-spaced street-lights flickered on, the tides of people flowed endlessly

title: Peter-Paul comes over
why: Reed “hurried to Smolny” after the film and left at three in the morning.
sum: In room 10 at Smolny, Lazimir of the Military Revolutionary Committee tells Reed the fortress garrison has joined them.
q: “Peter-Paul Fortress has just come over to us,” said he, with a pleased grin.

also.q: Amid cheers he announced that the Left Socialist Revolutionaries had agreed to send representatives into the Military Revolutionary Committee

tp: at three o’clock in the morning
title: Guns at Smolny’s door
sum: Leaving Smolny, Reed sees two rapid-firing guns mounted at the door and patrols at the gates.
q: As I left Smolny, at three o’clock in the morning, I noticed that two rapid-firing guns had been mounted, one on each side of the door

ref.q: two rapid-firing guns had been mounted, one on each side of the door
strong patrols of soldiers guarded the gates and the near-by street-corners

title: “We’re off!”
why: Shatov meets Reed on the steps as he leaves at three.
sum: Bill Shatov runs up the steps: the yunkers closed the Bolshevik papers, and Soviet troops have broken the government seals.
q: Kerensky sent the yunkers to close down our papers, Soldat and Rabotchi Put. But our troops went down and smashed the Government seals

title: Yunker batteries at the palace
why: After the morning papers, before Kerensky’s speech at the Mariinsky.
sum: Crossing Palace Square to the Foreign Office censor, Reed sees yunker artillery trot through the Red Arch and draw up before the Winter Palace.
q: As I crossed the Palace Square several batteries of yunker artillery came through the Red Arch at a jingling trot, and drew up before the Palace.

ref.q: several armoured automobiles ranked before the door, and motors full of officers were coming and going

title: Kerensky’s last speech
why: The censor says Kerensky “had just gone” to the Council.
sum: Reed reaches the Council of the Republic at the end of Kerensky’s long speech of self-justification.
q: I hurried down to the Marinsky Palace, arriving at the end of that passionate and almost incoherent speech of Kerensky’s, full of self-justification and bitter denunciation of his enemies.

title: Cars turned out
why: After the Council’s vote, before nightfall at Smolny.
sum: At the corner of the Morskaya and the Nevsky soldiers stop private cars, turn out the occupants and order them toward the Winter Palace; nobody knows whose soldiers they are.
q: At the corner of the Morskaya and the Nevsky, squads of soldiers with fixed bayonets were stopping all private automobiles, turning out the occupants, and ordering them toward the Winter Palace.

moves.size: ordering them toward the Winter Palace

present.size: squads of soldiers with fixed bayonets

ref.q: A large crowd had gathered to watch them.
stopping all private automobiles, turning out the occupants

title: “Cronstadt is coming!”
why: Straight after the scene at the Morskaya corner.
sum: In front of the Kazan Cathedral, sailors with Avrora and Zaria Svobody on their hat bands tell the soldiers the fleet is coming.
q: On the sailors’ hat bands were Avrora and Zaria Svobody
One of them said, “Cronstadt is coming!”

also.q: Up in front of the Kazan Cathedral the same thing was happening, machines being directed back up the Nevsky.

present.size: Five or six sailors with rifles

ref.q: Five or six sailors with rifles came along, laughing excitedly, and fell into conversation with two of the soldiers.

present.size: squads of soldiers with fixed bayonets

ref.q: stopping all private automobiles, turning out the occupants, and ordering them toward the Winter Palace. A large crowd had gathered to watch them. Nobody knew whether the soldiers belonged to the Government or the Military Revolutionary Committee. Up in front of the Kazan Cathedral the same thing was happening

title: Night at Smolny
sum: As night falls the great hall fills with soldiers and workmen for the old Tsay-ee-kah’s session, which is to welcome the delegates to the new Congress.
q: As night fell the great hall filled with soldiers and workmen, a monstrous dun mass, deep-humming in a blue haze of smoke.

title: Dan and Trotzky after midnight
sum: After midnight Gotz takes the chair and Dan rises to speak in a tense silence: “If the Bolsheviki start anything, that will be the end of the Revolution.” Then Trotzky mounts the tribune for the Bolsheviki, borne on roaring applause and a rising house.
q: It was after midnight when Gotz took the chair and Dan rose to speak, in a tense silence, which seemed to me almost menacing.

also.q: If the Bolsheviki start anything, that will be the end of the Revolution
Then for the Bolsheviki, Trotzky mounted the tribune, borne on a wave of roaring applause that burst into cheers and a rising house, thunderous.

present.size: soldiers and workmen, a monstrous dun mass

ref.q: As night fell the great hall filled with soldiers and workmen, a monstrous dun mass, deep-humming in a blue haze of smoke.

title: The Telegraph Agency occupied
sum: Reed’s chronology of the night: a detachment from Smolny takes the Petrograd Telegraph Agency.
q: At 1 A. M. a detachment of soldiers and sailors from Smolny occupied the Telegraph Agency.

moves.size: a detachment of soldiers and sailors

title: The Post Office occupied
sum: Reed’s chronology: the Main Post Office is occupied.
q: At 1.35 the Post Office was occupied.

title: The Bolsheviki walk out
why: Late in the session that began “after midnight”, just before Reed meets Zorin “toward four”.
sum: When the old Tsay-ee-kah moves to take on the Congress’s functions, the Bolsheviki leave the hall and the resolution passes.
q: Whereupon all the Bolsheviki left the hall and the resolution was passed

title: What the papers said
why: Dien reports the night’s captures in the paper of the 7th; the time is that of the captures, which the control change dates, not of the reading.
sum: The paper Dien reports the night: the Bolsheviki have taken the Telephone Exchange, the Baltic Station and the Telegraph Agency.
q: Bolsheviki capture of the Telephone Exchange, the Baltic station, the Telegraph Agency

title: “We ran all the way to Smolny”
why: After the arrests that began at half-past two (“In an hour we had some officers and a couple of Ministers”) and the order to let everybody go; they talk for an hour at Smolny and are back at the Staff at five.
sum: The Pavlovsky ensign’s story: ordered to let everybody go, the guards at the Staff run all the way to Smolny, and talk for an hour before the Military Revolutionary Committee finally sees that it is war.
q: Well, we ran all the way to Smolny, and I guess we talked for an hour before they finally saw that it was war.

also.q: But the Military Revolutionary Committee wasn’t ready; they didn’t know what to do; and pretty soon back came the order to let everybody go and not arrest anybody else.

moves.size: Some of my comrades and I

title: Kerensky at the Staff
sum: Reed’s chronology of 7 Nov: from four until dawn Kerensky stays at the Petrograd Staff Headquarters, while Colonel Polkovnikov, Commandant of the City, hurries between the Staff and the Winter Palace.
q: From 4 A. M. until dawn Kerensky remained at the Petrograd Staff Headquarters

also.q: Colonel Polkovnikov, Commandant of the City, hurried between the Staff and the Winter Palace, evidently without any plan.

title: “We’re moving!”
sum: Zorin, rifle on his shoulder, tells Reed ministers are arrested and regiments are marching on the Telephone Exchange, the Telegraph Agency and the State Bank.
q: Toward four in the morning I met Zorin in the outer hall
One regiment is on the march to capture the Telephone Exchange, another the Telegraph Agency, another the State Bank.

title: The Red Guard, and firing at the bridges
sum: On Smolny’s steps Reed first sees the Red Guard. Westward, rifle fire: yunkers trying to open the Neva bridges, sailors closing them.
q: On the steps of Smolny, in the chill dark, we first saw the Red Guard
Far over the still roofs westward came the sound of scattered rifle fire, where the yunkers were trying to open the bridges over the Neva

also.q: and the Cronstadt sailors were closing them again

present.size: a huddled group of boys in workmen’s clothes, carrying guns with bayonets

title: The Military Hotel taken
sum: Reed’s chronology: “toward morning” the Military Hotel, the Astoria, is taken.
q: Toward morning the Military Hotel was taken

title: Arrests at the Staff
sum: At Peter-Paul an ensign of the Pavlovsky Regiment, on guard at the Staff that night, tells Reed how it began: arrests from half-past two, halted by Smolny, resumed after a run to Smolny, too late for most.
q: It was five o’clock when we got back to the Staff, and by that time most of them were gone.

also.q: A praporshtchik of the Pavlovsky regiment was telling us how the insurrection started.

present.size: Some of my comrades and I

ref.q: Some of my comrades and I were standing guard

title: The Telephone Exchange taken
why: Reed gives five o’clock; one minute later than the Military Hotel only to keep the two in his order.
sum: Reed’s chronology: at five the Telephone Exchange is taken.
q: and at 5 o’clock the Telephone Exchange

title: The Nicolai Bridge opened
why: Three hours after an order given while Kerensky was at the Staff (from 4 a.m.).
sum: Three hours after Kerensky’s order to open the bridges, an officer and five men go out on their own initiative, put a picket of Red Guards to flight and open the Nicolai Bridge.
q: Kerensky gave an order to open the bridges; three hours passed without any action, and then an officer and five men went out on their own initiative, and putting to flight a picket of Red Guards, opened the Nicolai Bridge.

title: The Nicolai Bridge closed again
why: “Immediately after” the officer and five men left the bridge they had opened, three hours after Kerensky’s order to open the bridges, given at the Staff, where he was from 4 A.M.
sum: Immediately after the officer and his five men leave, some sailors close the Nicolai Bridge again.
q: Immediately after they left, however, some sailors closed it again.

title: An attempt to retake the Post Office
why: Reed’s chronology of the morning “From 4 A. M. until dawn” gives no hour; it lists the attempt after the Nicolai Bridge, opened three hours after Kerensky’s order, and before Kerensky leaves “About 9 A. M.”
sum: Reed’s chronology: an attempt is made to recapture the Post Office and the Telegraph Agency; a few shots are fired, and the Government troops announce that they will no longer oppose the Soviets.
q: An attempt was made to recapture the Post Office and the Telegraph Agency; a few shots were fired, and the Government troops announced that they would no longer oppose the Soviets.

title: The State Bank surrounded
sum: Reed’s chronology: at dawn the State Bank is surrounded.
q: At dawn the State Bank was surrounded.

also.q: One regiment is on the march to capture the Telephone Exchange, another the Telegraph Agency, another the State Bank.

title: Kerensky leaves for the front
sum: Reed’s chronology: about nine Kerensky leaves the capital for the front.
q: About 9 A. M. Kerensky left for the Front

ref.q: and of the cruiser Avrora, anchored in the Neva

title: A cordon round the Winter Palace
sum: Reed’s chronology: at ten a cordon of troops is drawn about the Winter Palace.
q: And at 10 A. M. a cordon of troops was drawn about the Winter Palace.

title: “No more Government”
sum: Reed rises late. At noon, walking down the Nevsky, he asks the soldiers at the State Bank’s gates whose side they are on.
q: The noon cannon boomed from Peter-Paul as I went down the Nevsky.
“No more Government,” one answered with a grin, “Slava Bogu! Glory to God!”

ref.q: In front of the State Bank some soldiers with fixed bayonets were standing at the closed gates.

title: Officers kept in the Military Hotel
why: After the State Bank and a talk with Gomberg at the Morskaya corner.
sum: Sailors picket the Military Hotel; the officers in its lobby are not allowed to leave. Outside a rifle cracks, then a scattered burst of firing, and Reed runs out.
q: The Military Hotel at the corner of St. Isaac’s Square was picketed by armed sailors.

also.q: In the lobby were many of the smart young officers, walking up and down or muttering together; the sailors wouldn’t let them leave
Suddenly came the sharp crack of a rifle outside, followed by a scattered burst of firing. I ran out.

present.size: many of the smart young officers

ref.q: In the lobby were many of the smart young officers, walking up and down or muttering together; the sailors wouldn’t let them leave

title: The Council of the Republic dispersed
why: Straight after the Military Hotel: “I ran out.”
sum: Something unusual at the Mariinsky Palace: a line of soldiers drawn diagonally across the square stares at the hotel roof (“Shot at us!”), an armoured car at the palace’s western corner trains its guns toward St. Isaac’s, and a barricade closes Novaya Ulitza. A sailor tells how they turned the Council out.
q: Something unusual was going on around the Marinsky Palace

also.q: “We walked in there,” he said, “and filled all the doors with comrades.
Diagonally across the wide square was drawn a line of soldiers, rifles ready, staring at the hotel roof.
“_Provacatzia!_ Shot at us!” snapped one, while another went running toward the door.
At the western corner of the Palace lay a big armoured car with a red flag flying from it
A barricade had been heaped up across the mouth of Novaya Ulitza—boxes, barrels, an old bed-spring, a wagon.

ref.q: A barricade had been heaped up across the mouth of Novaya Ulitza—boxes, barrels, an old bed-spring, a wagon. A pile of lumber barred the end of the Moika quay.

present.size: a crowd of soldiers and sailors

ref.q: Before the door of the Palace was a crowd of soldiers and sailors.

present.size: a line of soldiers, rifles ready

ref.q: Diagonally across the wide square was drawn a line of soldiers, rifles ready, staring at the hotel roof.

At the western corner of the Palace lay a big armoured car with a red flag flying from it, newly lettered in red paint: “S.R.S.D.” (_Soviet Rabotchikh Soldatskikh Deputatov_); all the guns trained toward St. Isaac’s.
Down the Voskressensky Prospect a great mass of sailors were drawn up, and behind them came marching soldiers, as far as the eye could reach.

present.size: marching soldiers, as far as the eye could reach

ref.q: Down the Voskressensky Prospect a great mass of sailors were drawn up, and behind them came marching soldiers, as far as the eye could reach.

title: Inside the besieged palace
why: After the Mariinsky, before “it was getting late”.
sum: Through the cordon by way of the Admiralteisky, on their American passports, Reed and others walk into the palace: a barracks of yunkers.
q: We went toward the Winter Palace by way of the Admiralteisky.

also.q: Machine guns were mounted on window-sills, rifles stacked between the mattresses.

ref.q: Except for far-away soldiers who seemed to be carrying wood out of the Palace courtyard and piling it in front of the main gateway, everything was quiet.
a cordon of troops stretched clear across the western end, besieged by an uneasy throng of citizens
a cordon of troops stretched clear across the western end, besieged by an uneasy throng of citizens
“Yes, they are in the back rooms, where they won’t be hurt if any trouble comes.”
All the entrances to the Palace Square were closed by sentries, and a cordon of troops stretched clear across the western end

title: A sortie through the Red Arch
why: Reed watches from a palace window, before dusk.
sum: Two of three companies of yunkers drawn up before the palace march off across the Square and through the Red Arch, “to capture the Telephone Exchange”, someone says.
q: went swinging off across the Square, disappearing through the Red Arch into the quiet city.
“They are going to capture the Telephone Exchange,” said some one.

also.q: For a while we stood at the window, looking down on the Square before the Palace

ref.q: looking down on the Square before the Palace, where three companies of long-coated yunkers were drawn up under arms

title: A burst of rifle-fire
why: After the sortie and the cadets’ talk at the window; before the yunkers come back.
sum: A burst of rifle-fire not far off: out on the Square the people run and throw themselves flat, the cab drivers gallop off, and inside the palace the yunkers grab their rifles. Reed does not see who fired.
q: At this point there was a burst of rifle-fire not far off. Out on the Square all the people began to run, falling flat on their faces, and the izvoshtchiki, standing on the corners, galloped in every direction.

also.q: Inside all was uproar, soldiers running here and there, grabbing up guns, rifle-belts and shouting

moves.size: the izvoshtchiki, standing on the corners
the izvoshtchiki, standing on the corners
the izvoshtchiki, standing on the corners

title: The yunkers come back
why: “In a few minutes” after the firing it was quiet; before “it was getting late when we left the Palace”.
sum: The yunkers come back through the Red Arch across the Square, a little out of step, one of them held up by two comrades.
q: Through the Red Arch appeared the yunkers, marching a little out of step, one of them supported by two comrades.

ref.q: The sentries in the Square had all disappeared.

title: Dinner at the Hotel France
why: “It was getting late when we left the Palace.”
sum: At dinner the pale waiter moves them to the back room: the café lights are going out, “there will be much shooting”.
q: We went into the Hotel France for dinner, and right in the middle of soup the waiter, very pale in the face, came up and insisted that we move to the main dining-room at the back of the house

title: Kerensky at Ostrov
sum: From Gatchina by special train, Kerensky is at Ostrov, Province of Pskov, toward evening.
q: Leaving Petrograd in the morning of November 7th, Kerensky arrived by automobile at Gatchina, where he demanded a special train.
Toward evening he was in Ostrov, Province of Pskov.

title: “The Women’s Battalion is in there”
why: After dinner, before the Police Bridge and the drive to Smolny.
sum: At the Red Arch soldiers stare at the lighted palace and argue against shooting.
q: “No, comrades,” one was saying. “How can we shoot at them? The Women’s Battalion is in there—they will say we have fired on Russian women.”

ref.q: We walked back up to the Red Arch, where a knot of soldiers was gathered staring at the brightly-lighted Winter Palace
Under this stood a big armored automobile, with racing engine and oil-smoke pouring out of it.

title: “The Committee says to wait”
why: When Reed comes back down from the Red Arch to the Nevsky; before the lumber-piles on the Police Bridge.
sum: Back at the Nevsky corner a second armoured car comes round, and a man in its turret yells to go on through and attack. The first car’s driver shouts above the engine that the Committee says to wait: they have artillery behind the wood-piles.
q: As we reached the Nevsky again another armoured car came around the corner, and a man poked his head out of the turret-top.

also.q: “The Committee says to wait. They have got artillery behind the wood-piles in there….”
“Come on!” he yelled. “Let’s go on through and attack!”
The driver of the other car came over, and shouted so as to be heard above the roaring engine.

ref.q: As we reached the Nevsky again another armoured car came around the corner, and a man poked his head out of the turret-top.

title: A field-gun on the Nevsky
why: Back on the Nevsky after the Red Arch.
sum: In the dark the Police Bridge is barricaded with lumber, and soldiers wheel a three-inch field-gun into place before the Stroganov Palace.
q: In the darkness we stumbled over lumber-piles barricading the Police Bridge, and before the Stroganov Palace made out some soldiers wheeling into position a three-inch field-gun.

title: A red spark on a roof
why: The last scene before Smolny.
sum: Up the Nevsky the whole city seems to be out promenading: crowds on every corner, pickets at the crossings, armoured cars going up and down, people fighting for newspapers at the Mikhailovsky. At the Sadovaya corner two thousand people stare at a red spark on a roof: “a provocator”, says a peasant.
q: On the corner of the Sadovaya about two thousand citizens had gathered, staring up at the roof of a tall building, where a tiny red spark glowed and waned.

also.q: Up the Nevsky the whole city seemed to be out promenading.
Armoured cars went up and down the street, named after the first Tsars—Oleg, Rurik, Svietoslav—and daubed with huge red letters, “R. S. D. R. P.”
At the Mikhailovsky a man appeared with an armful of newspapers, and was immediately stormed by frantic people, offering a rouble, five roubles, ten roubles, tearing at each other like animals.
“See!” said a tall peasant, pointing to it. “It is a provocator.

ref.q: On every corner immense crowds were massed around a core of hot discussion.

present.size: Pickets of a dozen soldiers with fixed bayonets

ref.q: Pickets of a dozen soldiers with fixed bayonets lounged at the street-crossings
Armoured cars went up and down the street, named after the first Tsars—Oleg, Rurik, Svietoslav—and daubed with huge red letters, “R. S. D. R. P.”
At the Mikhailovsky a man appeared with an armful of newspapers, and was immediately stormed by frantic people, offering a rouble, five roubles, ten roubles, tearing at each other like animals.

title: The Second Congress opens
sum: Dan rings the bell to open the Second All-Russian Congress of Soviets: his party comrades, he says, are in the Winter Palace under bombardment. Later a new sound is heard in the hall: the dull shock of guns.
q: It was 10.40 P. M. Dan, a mild-faced, baldish figure in a shapeless military surgeon’s uniform, was ringing the bell.

also.q: at this very moment our party comrades are in the Winter Palace under bombardment
But suddenly a new sound made itself heard, deeper than the tumult of the crowd, persistent, disquieting,—the dull shock of guns.

ref.q: It was cold, and at the outer gate the Red Guards had built themselves a bon-fire.

present.size: the four rapid-fire guns on each side of the doorway

ref.q: The canvas covers had been taken off the four rapid-fire guns on each side of the doorway, and the ammunition-belts hung snakelike from their breeches.
A dun herd of armoured cars stood under the trees in the court-yard, engines going.
At the inner gate, too, there was a blaze, by the light of which the sentries slowly spelled out our passes and looked us up and down.
So we came into the great meeting-hall, pushing through the clamorous mob at the door.

title: The moderates walk out
why: Late in the opening session, before the MRC room and the truck.
sum: Abramovitch: the Bund joins the Mensheviki and SRs in leaving the Congress, to “perish with the Provisional Government”.
q: The Bund group joins with the declaration of the Mensheviki and Socialist Revolutionaries and will leave the Congress!

ref.q: So we came into the great meeting-hall, pushing through the clamorous mob at the door.

title: Men over a map
why: Just before Reed leaves Smolny on the truck.
sum: Through the door of the Military Revolutionary Committee Reed glimpses men bent over a map. Outside, the front of Smolny is one huge park of automobiles, and a great motor-truck stands there, its engine roaring.
q: we caught a glimpse of dishevelled men bending over a map under the glare of a shaded electric-light

also.q: all the front of Smolny was one huge park of arriving and departing automobiles
A great motor-truck stood there, shaking to the roar of its engine.

present.size: Men were tossing bundles into it, and others receiving them

ref.q: all the front of Smolny was one huge park of arriving and departing automobiles, above the sound of which could be heard the far-off slow beat of the cannon. A great motor-truck stood there, shaking to the roar of its engine.

title: Proclamations from a truck
why: After the passes are made out at Smolny, before the Duma march.
sum: On an MRC truck Reed helps fling the proclamation of the Provisional Government’s fall into the streets, down the Suvorovsky and the Nevsky, until a line of sailors beyond the lighted Duma yells at it to stop.
q: We imitated him, plunging down through the dark street with a tail of white papers floating and eddying out behind.

also.q: We turned into Znamensky Square, dark and almost deserted
The City Duma was all brightly lighted. Beyond that we made out a dark mass of people, and a line of sailors, who yelled furiously at us to stop.

ref.q: The City Duma was all brightly lighted. Beyond that we made out a dark mass of people, and a line of sailors, who yelled furiously at us to stop.

title: The march to die in the Winter Palace
why: When Reed’s truck stops at the cordon beyond the Duma; before the procession turns back.
sum: The Duma, the Mayor and the Mensheviki and SRs set out to die with the ministers. A cordon of sailors drawn across the Nevsky stops their column of fours at the Ekaterina Canal, under 200 m from the Duma door.
q: “Going to die in the Winter Palace,” he shouted cheerfully.

also.q: “We will spank you!” he cried, energetically.
a cordon of armed sailors was drawn across the Nevsky, blocking the way to a crowd of people in column of fours

ref.q: Just at the corner of the Ekaterina Canal, under an arc-light, a cordon of armed sailors was drawn across the Nevsky, blocking the way to a crowd of people in column of fours.

present.size: about three or four hundred of them

ref.q: Just at the corner of the Ekaterina Canal, under an arc-light, a cordon of armed sailors was drawn across the Nevsky, blocking the way to a crowd of people in column of fours.

title: The procession turns back
why: After the argument at the cordon and Prokopovitch’s speech; Reed then walks on to the Morskaya, where the storming begins.
sum: In dignified silence the procession marches back up the Nevsky in column of fours. Reed slips past the guards toward the Winter Palace: in front of the Kazan Cathedral a field-gun lies slewed in the street, soldiers in the doorways peer toward the Police Bridge, and the shooting has ceased.
q: Whereupon, in dignified silence, the procession marched around and back up the Nevsky, always in column of fours.

also.q: And taking advantage of the diversion we slipped past the guards and set off in the direction of the Winter Palace.
In front of the Kazan Cathedral a three-inch field-gun lay in the middle of the street, slewed sideways from the recoil of its last shot over the roofs.
Soldiers were standing in every doorway talking in low tones and peering down toward the Police Bridge.
The shooting had ceased.

ref.q: Just at the corner of the Ekaterina Canal, under an arc-light, a cordon of armed sailors was drawn across the Nevsky, blocking the way to a crowd of people in column of fours.
In front of the Kazan Cathedral a three-inch field-gun lay in the middle of the street, slewed sideways from the recoil of its last shot over the roofs.

present.size: Soldiers were standing in every doorway

ref.q: Soldiers were standing in every doorway talking in low tones and peering down toward the Police Bridge.

present.size: pickets of soldiers and Red Guards

ref.q: Here it was absolutely dark, and nothing moved but pickets of soldiers and Red Guards grimly intent.

title: Through the Red Arch
why: Reed gives no hour for the entry; he leaves the palace “after three in the morning”.
sum: At the Morskaya word comes that the yunkers want to be got out. In silence, like a black river, the column pours through the Red Arch, runs across the open stooping low, and jams up behind the pedestal of the Alexander Column.
q: Like a black river, filling all the street, without song or cheer we poured through the Red Arch
jammed up suddenly behind the pedestal of the Alexander Column

also.q: Just as we came to the Morskaya somebody was shouting: “The yunkers have sent word they want us to go and get them out!”
Look out, comrades! Don't trust them. They will fire, surely!
In the open we began to run, stooping low and bunching together

ref.q: Over the barricade of firewood we clambered, and leaping down inside gave a triumphant shout as we stumbled on a heap of rifles thrown down by the yunkers who had stood there.
In the open we began to run, stooping low and bunching together, and jammed up suddenly behind the pedestal of the Alexander Column.

title: Over the barricade
why: “After a few minutes huddling there” behind the Alexander Column; before the looting in the cellar of the East wing.
sum: After a few minutes the mass flows forward again, Red Guards with only a few soldiers. Over the barricade of firewood lies a heap of rifles the yunkers threw down; the doors on both sides of the main gateway stand open, the palace is silent, and the wave sweeps Reed in at the right-hand entrance.
q: After a few minutes huddling there, some hundreds of men, the army seemed reassured and without any orders suddenly began again to flow forward.
Over the barricade of firewood we clambered, and leaping down inside gave a triumphant shout as we stumbled on a heap of rifles thrown down by the yunkers who had stood there.

also.q: the first two or three hundred men were Red Guards, with only a few scattered soldiers
On both sides of the main gateway the doors stood wide open, light streamed out, and from the huge pile came not the slightest sound.
Carried along by the eager wave of men we were swept into the right hand entrance, opening into a great bare vaulted room, the cellar of the East wing

moves.size: the first two or three hundred men were Red Guards, with only a few scattered soldiers

present.size: the first two or three hundred men were Red Guards, with only a few scattered soldiers

ref.q: Carried along by the eager wave of men we were swept into the right hand entrance, opening into a great bare vaulted room, the cellar of the East wing

title: “Property of the People!”
why: Just after the entry.
sum: In the cellar the looting starts and is stopped by the crowd itself. At the door the Army pours out, and yunkers coming out in bunches of three or four are disarmed and let go.
q: “Comrades! Don’t touch anything! Don’t take anything! This is the property of the People!”

also.q: the Army began to pour through the door, jostling, expostulating, arguing
Yunkers came out, in bunches of three or four.
The yunkers were disarmed.
Whereupon they were allowed to go free.

present.size: in bunches of three or four

ref.q: Yunkers came out, in bunches of three or four.

title: The ministers taken to Peter-Paul
why: “It was only later that we learned…”
sum: The arrested ministers, half a dozen men in civilian dress, are led out in single file. A crowd in the street wants to lynch them and shots are fired, but the sailors get them to Peter-Paul.
q: the sailors brought them safely to Peter-Paul

also.q: After them followed single file half a dozen men in civilian dress--the members of the Provisional Government.
It was only later that we learned how the people in the street wanted to lynch them, and shots were fired

moves.size: half a dozen men in civilian dress

title: The Women’s Battalion
why: Told on the quay as Reed leaves the palace, just before “It was now after three in the morning”.
sum: A Commissar tells Reed the women soldiers were found huddled in a back room, marched to the Finland Station and sent to their camp at Levashovo.
q: So finally we marched them up to the Finland Station and put them on a train for Levashovo, where they have a camp.

tp: It was now after three in the morning
title: Broken stucco
sum: Leaving the palace, Reed walks over stucco knocked off the cornice, “the only damage done by the bombardment”.
q: Underfoot the sidewalk was littered with broken stucco, from the cornice of the Palace where two shells from the battleship Avrora had struck
It was now after three in the morning.

present.size: Red Guards and soldiers squatting around fires

ref.q: the only signs of war were Red Guards and soldiers squatting around fires
On the Nevsky all the street-lights were again shining, the cannon gone
On the Nevsky all the street-lights were again shining, the cannon gone, and the only signs of war were Red Guards and soldiers squatting around fires
On the Nevsky all the street-lights were again shining, the cannon gone

title: The Committee for Salvation is formed
why: Reed walks from the palace to the Duma “after three”.
sum: In the Duma’s Alexander Hall, on Skobeliev’s motion, the anti-Bolshevik groups form the Committee for Salvation of Country and Revolution.
q: We mounted to the galleried Alexander Hall
And as we looked on, the Committee for Salvation was formed

title: The Internationalists leave
why: After Reed’s cab from the Duma, where he saw the Committee for Salvation formed after three, and the speeches that greet his arrival; before the appeal is read and Krylenko’s telegram at 5:17.
sum: Reed’s cab from the Duma stops two blocks short of Smolny. In the hall Kapelinski’s motion for a peaceful solution is voted down, and the Menshevik Internationalists leave the Congress “in a Whirlwind of Jocular insults”.
q: The vote was overwhelmingly against, and the Mensheviki Internationalists left the Congress in a Whirlwind of Jocular insults.

also.q: he wanted thirty rubles, and stopped two blocks away
The windows of Smolny were still ablaze, motors came and went, and around the still-leaping fires the sentries huddled close

ref.q: So we came into the great meeting-hall, pushing through the clamorous mob at the door.

title: The Twelfth Army goes over
sum: Krylenko reads a telegram: the Twelfth Army’s new Military Revolutionary Committee has taken command of the Northern Front.
q: It was exactly 5:17 A.M. when Krylenko, staggering with fatigue, climbed to the tribune with a telegram in his hand.

ref.q: So we came into the great meeting-hall, pushing through the clamorous mob at the door.

title: The Duma in permanence
sum: In the Nicolai Hall the Duma sits in permanence, gathering the opposition; Mayor Schreider describes his protest at Smolny.
q: In the high, amphitheatrical Nicolai Hall that afternoon I saw the Duma sitting in permanence, tempestuous, grouping around it all the forces of opposition.

title: Hand-bills at the Duma’s door
why: After the afternoon sitting and the news and rumours, which Reed carries on to “toward nightfall”; before the corner of the Liteiny and the evening session at Smolny.
sum: As Reed leaves the Duma building, two boy scouts are distributing hand-bills to the enormous crowd that blocks the Nevsky in front of the door, a crowd almost entirely of business men, shop-keepers, tchinouniki and clerks.
q: As we left the Duma building two boy scouts were distributing hand-bills

also.q: to the enormous crowd which blocked the Nevsky in front of the door—a crowd composed almost entirely of business men, shop-keepers, tchinouniki, clerks

present.size: a crowd composed almost entirely of business men, shop-keepers, tchinouniki, clerks

ref.q: to the enormous crowd which blocked the Nevsky in front of the door—a crowd composed almost entirely of business men, shop-keepers, tchinouniki, clerks

title: Menshevik papers seized
why: Between the Duma that afternoon and the evening session at Smolny.
sum: At the corner of the Liteiny, Red Guards and sailors take a news-dealer’s Menshevik papers; an ugly crowd gathers.
q: Up on the corner of the Liteiny, five or six Red Guards and a couple of sailors had surrounded a news-dealer and were demanding that he hand over his copies of the Menshevik Rabot-chaya Gazeta

present.size: five or six Red Guards and a couple of sailors

ref.q: An ugly crowd had gathered around, abusing the patrol.

title: Lenin
sum: The presidium enters to a wave of cheers, Lenin among them. “We shall now proceed to construct the Socialist order!”
q: It was just 8.40 when a thundering wave of cheers announced the entrance of the presidium, with Lenin—great Lenin—among them.

also.q: “We shall now proceed to construct the Socialist order!”

ref.q: So we came into the great meeting-hall, pushing through the clamorous mob at the door.

title: The proclamation on peace
sum: The Congress votes the proclamation to the peoples on peace; one hand goes up against and comes down again.
q: It was exactly 10:35 when Kameniev asked all in favour of the proclamation to hold up their cards.

ref.q: So we came into the great meeting-hall, pushing through the clamorous mob at the door.

title: Kerensky at Luga
sum: Shouted down by the soldiers at Ostrov and kept from Pskov, Kerensky reaches Luga by car on the night of 8 Nov.
q: Kerensky did not arrive at Pskov.
On the night of November 8th he arrived by automobile at Luga, where he was well received by the Death Battalions stationed there.

title: The Land Decree
sum: The Land Decree passes with one vote against, the peasant delegates wild with joy.
q: At two o’clock the Land Decree was put to vote, with only one against and the peasant delegates wild with joy.

ref.q: So we came into the great meeting-hall, pushing through the clamorous mob at the door.

title: The Council of People’s Commissars
sum: Kameniev reads the decree forming the Council of People’s Commissars.
q: At 2.30 A. M. fell a tense hush. Kameniev was reading the decree of the Constitution of Power

ref.q: So we came into the great meeting-hall, pushing through the clamorous mob at the door.

title: Gatchina falls to Kerensky
why: “During the night” before Friday the 9th.
sum: Gatchina falls in the night to Kerensky’s “loyal regiments”, Krasnov’s Cossacks, and becomes his headquarters.
q: Gatchina, about thirty kilometers south-west, had fallen during the night.

also.q: The town of Gatchina has been taken by the loyal regiments without bloodshed.

title: Home by the delegates’ tram
sum: Near seven, Reed rides home on the trams kept at Smolny for the delegates; at his apartment-house an armed citizens’ patrol stops them.
q: It was almost seven when we woke the sleeping conductors and motor-men
At our apartment-house we were held up in the dark by an armed patrol of citizens and carefully examined.

title: At the Duma’s doors
why: Reed comes down the Nevsky “a little after midday”; the Duma is surrounded that afternoon.
sum: A handful of armed workers and soldiers come to seize the Duma’s papers and are mobbed by a well-dressed crowd shouting “Traitors!”
q: On one side a handful of workmen and common soldiers, with arms in their hands, representing a victorious insurrection—and perfectly miserable

also.q: As we came down the Nevsky a little after midday the whole street before the Duma building was crowded with people.

present.size: students and officers with white arm-bands

ref.q: The doors were guarded by students and officers with white arm-bands lettered in red

present.size: Red Guards and sailors, with bayonetted rifles

ref.q: Here and there stood Red Guards and sailors, with bayonetted rifles, each one surrounded by about a hundred men and women

present.size: the kind of people that crowd the sidewalks of Fifth Avenue

ref.q: on the other a frantic mob made up of the kind of people that crowd the sidewalks of Fifth Avenue at noon-time

title: A shot into the crowd
why: Moments before the armoured car: Reed is still at the window when it comes round the corner (“As we looked, suddenly”).
sum: Outside the Duma a Red Guard, exasperated by the crowd’s taunts, has fired into it and wounded a young girl in the arm. From the windows Reed sees her lifted into a cab, an excited throng round her.
q: A Red Guard, finally exasperated by the taunts of the crowd, had shot into it, wounding a young girl in the arm.

also.q: Outside there was a shot. We ran to the windows.
We could see her being lifted into a cab, surrounded by an excited throng, the clamour of whose voices floated up to us.

ref.q: each one surrounded by about a hundred men and women—clerks, students, shopkeepers, _tchinovniki_—shaking their fists and bawling insults and menaces.

title: An armoured car at the Duma
why: Between the scene at the doors and the Duma’s emergency session.
sum: After a Red Guard wounds a girl, an armoured car swings round the corner of the Mikhailovsky and the crowd throws itself down.
q: suddenly an armoured automobile appeared around the corner of the Mikhailovsky, its guns sluing this way and that.

also.q: Immediately the crowd began to run, as Petrograd crowds do, falling down and lying still in the street, piled in the gutters, heaped up behind telephone-poles.
The car lumbered up to the steps of the Duma and a man stuck his head out of the turret, demanding the surrender of the _Soldatski Golos._

present.size: some hundreds of men and women

ref.q: Immediately the crowd began to run, as Petrograd crowds do, falling down and lying still in the street, piled in the gutters, heaped up behind telephone-poles.
The boy-scouts jeered and scuttled into the building.

title: Off up the Nevsky
why: “After a moment”, once the car had demanded the surrender of the Soldatski Golos.
sum: The car wheels undecidedly round and goes off up the Nevsky, and the people who threw themselves down pick themselves up and dust their clothes.
q: After a moment the automobile wheeled undecidedly around and went off up the Nevsky, while some hundreds of men and women picked themselves up and began to dust their clothes

present.size: some hundreds of men and women

title: “It is all a mistake”
why: Before dusk, when the cyclists come riding on the Nevsky.
sum: The Duma, believing itself surrounded, sits in emergency session; Riazanov, Bolshevik councillor, says the troops will be withdrawn.
q: It is all a mistake. I told the Mayor this morning that the Duma would be left alone

title: Cyclists on the Nevsky
sum: At dusk a double file of cyclists, come from the front to back the Soviets, comes riding on the Nevsky and halts; the crowd presses in with questions.
q: Out on the Nevsky, in the deepening dusk, a long double file of cyclists came riding, guns slung on their shoulders.

moves.size: a long double file of cyclists

present.size: a long double file of cyclists

ref.q: They halted, and the crowd pressed in and deluged them with questions.

title: “Will you give it back?”
why: After the cyclists at dusk, before Reed returns to the Duma.
sum: In the dim Mikhailovsky Riding School Krylenko, close to collapse, talks the two thousand armoured-car men out of neutrality.
q: The Government is in your hands. You are the masters. Great Russia belongs to you. Will you give it back?

ref.q: Inside only a single arc-light burned dimly, high up near the roof of the enormous hall, whose lofty pilasters and rows of windows vanished in the gloom. Around dimly squatted the monstrous shapes of the armoured cars.

title: Two commissions
why: Just before Reed reaches Peter-Paul at midnight.
sum: Back at the Duma, a commission goes with the Mayor to Peter-Paul to look into the yunkers’ treatment, and another is named to meet Kerensky.
q: As we followed them out, the Duma was appointing another commission to meet Kerensky

also.q: A commission composed of members of all parties was immediately appointed, and with the Mayor, sent to Peter Paul to investigate.

title: Into the fortress at midnight
sum: Reed bluffs his way into Peter-Paul behind the Duma’s commission, past the Tsars’ tombs, to the yunkers and the arrested ministers.
q: It was midnight when we bluffed our past the guards at the gate of the fortress

title: A column to battle with Kerensky
why: “After-midnight”, on the way back from Peter-Paul.
sum: After midnight an endless column of soldiers shuffles up the Nevsky in silence, going to meet Kerensky.
q: Up the Nevsky, in the empty after-midnight gloom, an interminable column of soldiers shuffled in silence—to battle with Kerensky.

title: Bulletin from Krasnoye Selo
why: Posted after the 8 a.m. bulletin and before Reed leaves for Tsarskoye.
sum: At Smolny they paste up a bulletin from Krasnoye Selo calling Kerensky’s telegram false; the garrisons of Gatchina, Pavlovsk and Tsarskoye are falling back.
q: In the halls they were pasting up bulletins

title: The city pours out to dig trenches
why: The afternoon the trench order went out.
sum: At the order to dig trenches the factory whistles blow, and men, women and children stream through the slums toward the Moskovsky Gate, companies of soldiers, guns and motor-trucks borne along with them.
q: South and southwest they poured through the shabby streets toward the Moskovsky Gate, men, women and children, with rifles, picks, spades, rolls of wire

also.q: They rolled along torrent-like, companies of soldiers borne with them, guns, motor-trucks, wagons

title: Antonov inspects the trenches
why: Reed hears it from Trusishka, who went with them; Reed himself “made for the Tsarskoye Selo station”.
sum: Antonov and Dybenko drive from Smolny to the Narva Gate. A tyre bursts on the Nevsky, so they take an Italian-flagged taxi. A few hundred workmen wait in trenches for the Cossacks.
q: Arrived at Narvskaya Zastava, about ten miles out, Antonov called for the commandant of the Red Guard.

ref.q: He was led to the edge of the town, where some few hundred workmen had dug trenches and were waiting for the Cossacks.

tp: The early twilight of winter was falling
title: “Peace! Land!”
sum: On the way to the Tsarskoye Selo station Reed passes young Red Guards marching up the Nevsky under a gold-lettered red flag.
q: A red flag crudely lettered in gold, “Peace! Land!” floated over them. They were very young.

also.q: Up the Nevsky, as we passed, Red Guards were marching, all armed, some with bayonets and some without.
Heads up they tramped in the chill mud, irregular lines of four, without music, without drums.

ref.q: Half-fearful, half-contemptuous, the crowds on the sidewalk watched them pass, in hateful silence

title: “Holding the city for Kerensky”
why: After the twilight walk up the Nevsky and the train out.
sum: Reed takes the train to Tsarskoye Selo. The Soviet has gone, the guards say they are “neutral”, and in the Ekaterina Palace the Colonel says he is holding the town for Kerensky, then takes it back.
q: “Oh dear no.” He smiled. “We are holding the city for Kerensky.”

also.q: Tsarskoye Selo station was quiet, but knots of soldiers stood here and there talking in low tones and looking uneasily down the empty track in the direction of Gatchina.
“The Soviet went away two days ago,” said he.
“Well, not exactly for Kerensky.” The Colonel hesitated.

title: Back in town
why: After the train back from Tsarskoye.
sum: Back in town, Reed finds excited throngs moving in tides up and down the Nevsky.
q: Back in town excited throngs were moving in tides up and down the Nevsky.

title: Cannon heard at the Warsaw Station
why: Reed gives it just after “Back in town”, before he goes to the Duma; no clock time.
sum: From the Warsaw Railway station a far-off cannonade can be heard.
q: From the Warsaw Railway station could be heard far-off cannonade.

title: A state of siege
why: Posted in the street as Reed leaves the Duma, the night of the 10th, just before “As we went home”.
sum: As Reed leaves the Duma a company of Red Guards marches down the dark, deserted street with a dozen prisoners. Podvoisky’s order declares Petrograd and its suburbs in a state of siege and forbids meetings in the open air.
q: are declared in a state of siege. All assemblies or meetings in the streets, and generally in the open air, are forbidden until further orders.

also.q: As we left the Duma a company of Red Guards, stern-faced and desperate, came marching down the dark, deserted street with a dozen prisoners

ref.q: As we left the Duma a company of Red Guards, stern-faced and desperate, came marching down the dark, deserted street with a dozen prisoners

tp: In the small hours of the morning
title: Yunkers take the Telephone Exchange
sum: Before the guard changes, yunkers disguised as Semionovsky soldiers take the Telephone Exchange with the Bolshevik password, and capture Antonov.
q: In the small hours of the morning a company of yunkers, disguised as soldiers of the Semionovsky Regiment, presented themselves at the Telephone Exchange just before the hour of changing guard.

also.q: They had the Bolshevik password, and took charge without arousing suspicion.
A few minutes later Antonov appeared, making a round of inspection. Him they captured and locked in a small room.

present.size: disguised as soldiers of the Semionovsky Regiment

title: A blast of rifle-fire
why: At the change of guard, after the yunkers had taken charge and, “a few minutes later”, captured Antonov.
sum: When the relief comes to the Telephone Exchange, now in the yunkers’ hands, it is met by a blast of rifle-fire; several are killed. Counter-revolution has begun.
q: When the relief came it was met by a blast of rifle-fire, several being killed.

also.q: Counter-revolution had begun

title: The Cossacks enter Tsarskoye Selo
why: “Next morning”; Kerensky’s seven o’clock ultimatum to the Rifles comes from inside the town.
sum: Krasnov’s Cossacks ride into Tsarskoye Selo, Kerensky on a white horse and the church bells ringing.
q: Next morning, Sunday the 11th, the Cossacks entered Tsarskoye Selo, Kerensky
himself riding a white horse and all the church-bells clamouring.

title: The Rifles shelled
sum: Kerensky gives the 2nd Tsarskoye Selo Rifles ten minutes to disarm; Cossack guns open on their barracks, and Tsarskoye’s soldiers are no longer neutral.
q: At seven in the morning he sent word to the Second Tsarskoye Selo Rifles to lay down their arms.

also.q: From that moment there were no more “neutral” soldiers in Tsarskoye.

title: Ultimatum to the Vladimir school
sum: A patrol of soldiers, sailors and Red Guards gives the Vladimir yunkers twenty minutes to lay down their arms; they refuse.
q: At seven in the morning the Vladimir yunker school was visited by a patrol of soldiers, sailors and Red Guards, who gave the yunkers twenty minutes to lay down their arms.

also.q: The ultimatum was rejected.

present.size: a patrol of soldiers, sailors and Red Guards

ref.q: At dawn the Military Hotel and the Telegraph Agency had been taken by large forces of _yunkers,_

title: The yunkers strike in the city
sum: Petrograd wakes to rifle-fire: at dawn large forces of yunkers take the Military Hotel and the Telegraph Agency.
q: At dawn the Military Hotel and the Telegraph Agency had been taken by large forces of yunkers,

also.q: Petrograd woke to bursts of rifle-fire, and the tramping thunder of men marching.

title: The yunkers driven back
why: “An hour later” than the seven o’clock ultimatum.
sum: An hour after the ultimatum the Vladimir yunkers try to march out and are driven back by fire from the corner of the Grebetskaya and the Bolshoy Prospekt.
q: An hour later the yunkers got ready to march, but were driven back by a violent fusillade from the corner of the Grebetskaya and the Bolshoy Prospekt.

title: The school surrounded
why: After the yunkers are driven back at eight; before the field-pieces arrive at half-past eleven.
sum: Soviet troops surround the Vladimir school and open fire, two armoured cars cruising back and forth raking it with machine guns. The yunkers telephone for help; the Cossacks dare not come, for a large body of sailors with two cannon commands their barracks.
q: Soviet troops surrounded the building and opened fire, two armoured cars cruising back and forth with machine guns raking it.

also.q: The _yunkers_ telephoned for help. The Cossacks replied that they dare not come, because a large body of sailors with two cannon commanded their barracks.

title: Bloodily recaptured
why: Reed gives no hour, only the order of events.
sum: The Military Hotel and the Telegraph Agency are retaken from the yunkers. Reed does not say by whom: the map draws sailors, who held the hotel before, storming both buildings while the yunkers fire from the windows.
q: and bloodily recaptured.

also.q: Petrograd woke to bursts of rifle-fire, and the tramping thunder of men marching.

title: The Telephone Station besieged
why: Reed’s account of the morning.
sum: Sailors besiege the Telephone Station from barricades of barrels and tin in the middle of the Morskaya and from the corners of the Gorokhovaya and St Isaac’s Square.
q: The Telephone Station was besieged by sailors, who lay behind barricades of barrels, boxes and tin sheets in the middle of the Morskaya

also.q: or sheltered themselves at the corner of the Gorokhovaya and of St. Isaac's Square, shooting at anything that moved

present.size: barricades of barrels, boxes and tin sheets

ref.q: or sheltered themselves at the corner of the Gorokhovaya and of St. Isaac’s Square, shooting at anything that moved

present.size: their dashing young defenders, the yunkers

ref.q: Romantic had been their experience passing up cartridges and dressing the wounds of their dashing young defenders, the _yunkers,_

title: A Red Cross car
why: During the siege, before the storming in the afternoon.
sum: Williams, inside the Exchange, rides out in a Red Cross car “ostensibly full of wounded”, which goes by devious ways to the yunkers’ headquarters.
q: Albert Rhys Williams was in the Telephone Exchange. He went out with the Red Cross automobile, which was ostensibly full of wounded.

also.q: Occasionally an automobile passed in and out, flying the Red Cross flag.
After circulating about the city, the car went by devious ways to the Mikhailovsky _yunker_ school, headquarters of the counter-revolution.

title: Field-guns at the Vladimir school
sum: Three field-pieces arrive. Another demand to surrender is met by the yunkers shooting down two of the Soviet delegates under the white flag.
q: At half-past eleven three field-pieces arrived.

also.q: Another demand to surrender was met by the _yunkers_ shooting down two of the Soviet delegates under the white flag.

ref.q: At half-past eleven three field-pieces arrived.
Soviet troops surrounded the building and opened fire, two armoured cars cruising back and forth with machine guns raking it.
Another demand to surrender was met by the _yunkers_ shooting down two of the Soviet delegates under the white flag.
Another demand to surrender was met by the _yunkers_ shooting down two of the Soviet delegates under the white flag.

title: Seven dead in an archway
why: During the day’s street fighting; no hour given.
sum: A yunker armoured car rolling up from the Admiralty stalls at the corner of the Gogolia. Sailors ambushed behind wood-piles open fire; its machine-gun sprays the wood-piles and the crowd, and seven people are shot dead in an archway. The sailors rush it and thrust their bayonets into its loop-holes.
q: In the archway where Miss Bryant stood seven people were shot dead, among them two little boys.

also.q: Five or six armoured cars, belonging to the disbanded British Armoured Car Division, were in their hands. As Louise Bryant was going along St. Isaac’s Square one came rolling up from the Admiralty, on its way to the Telephone Exchange.

At the corner of the Gogolia, right in front of her, the engine stalled. Some sailors ambushed behind wood-piles began shooting. The machine-gun in the turret of the thing slewed around and spat a hail of bullets indiscriminately into the wood-piles and the crowd.
Suddenly, with a shout, the sailors leaped up and rushed into the flaming open; closing around the monster, they thrust their bayonets into the loop-holes, again and again, yelling

ref.q: Some sailors ambushed behind wood-piles began shooting.

present.size: seven people were shot dead, among them two little boys

title: A real bombardment
why: After the demand to surrender that followed the guns at half-past eleven; before the white flag at half-past two.
sum: A real bombardment begins, and great holes are torn in the school’s walls. The yunkers defend themselves desperately; shouting waves of Red Guards crumple under their fire. Frenzied by their heaps of dead, the Soviet troops open a tornado of steel and flame that their own officers cannot stop.
q: Now began a real bombardment. Great holes were torn in the walls of the school.

also.q: The _yunkers_ defended themselves desperately; shouting waves of Red Guards, assaulting, crumpled under the withering blast
Frenzied by defeat and their heaps of dead, the Soviet troops opened a tornado of steel and flame against the battered building.
Their own officers could not stop the terrible bombardment.

ref.q: Soviet troops surrounded the building and opened fire, two armoured cars cruising back and forth with machine guns raking it.
Frenzied by defeat and their heaps of dead, the Soviet troops opened a tornado of steel and flame against the battered building.

title: The Vladimir school stormed
sum: At half-past two the yunkers hoist a white flag. With a rush and a shout thousands of soldiers and Red Guards pour through windows, doors and holes in the wall, and before it can be stopped five yunkers are beaten and stabbed to death.
q: At half-past two the yunkers hoisted a white flag
With a rush and a shout thousands of soldiers and Red Guards poured through windows, doors and holes in the wall.

also.q: Before it could be stopped five _yunkers_ were beaten and stabbed to death.

present.size: thousands of soldiers and Red Guards

ref.q: With a rush and a shout thousands of soldiers and Red Guards poured through windows, doors and holes in the wall.
Soviet troops surrounded the building and opened fire, two armoured cars cruising back and forth with machine guns raking it.
At half-past two the _yunkers_ hoisted a white flag
Before it could be stopped five _yunkers_ were beaten and stabbed to death.

title: To Peter-Paul under escort
why: After the storming at half-past two; before the victors march on the Injinierny Zamok “two hours later”.
sum: The rest of the Vladimir yunkers, about two hundred, are taken to Peter-Paul under escort in small groups; on the way a mob sets upon one party and kills eight more. More than a hundred Red Guards and soldiers have fallen.
q: The rest, about two hundred, were taken to Peter-Paul under escort, in small groups so as to avoid notice.

also.q: On the way a mob set upon one party, killing eight more _yunkers_
More than a hundred Red Guards and soldiers had fallen

title: The Exchange stormed
why: “Until afternoon”.
sum: A Bolshevik armoured car arrives and the sailors storm the Exchange. Williams brokers Antonov’s release, and the yunkers go free.
q: The Telephone Exchange held out until afternoon, when a Bolshevik armoured car appeared, and the sailors stormed the place.

also.q: Williams offered to mediate if Antonov were released. This was immediately done

ref.q: The Telephone Exchange held out until afternoon, when a Bolshevik armoured car appeared, and the sailors stormed the place.
The Telephone Exchange held out until afternoon, when a Bolshevik armoured car appeared, and the sailors stormed the place.

title: The last schools give up
why: “Two hours later” than the Vladimir surrender at half-past two.
sum: Two hours after the Vladimir school the victors march toward the Engineers’ Castle, and a dozen Duma members set out to hand them the Committee for Salvation’s latest proclamation. The other schools surrender without resistance.
q: Two hours later the Duma got a telephone message that the victors were marching toward the Injinierny Zamok
All the other schools surrendered without resistance

also.q: A dozen members immediately set out to distribute among them armfuls of the latest proclamation of the Committee for Salvation.

title: Sent unharmed to Peter-Paul and Cronstadt
why: After the schools had surrendered, which Reed tells after the victors’ march on the Engineers’ Castle.
sum: The yunkers of the schools that surrendered are sent unharmed to Peter-Paul and to Cronstadt.
q: the yunkers were sent unharmed to Peter-Paul and Cronstadt

title: Debate at the Kazan Cathedral
sum: At dusk on the almost empty Nevsky a crowd argues before the Kazan Cathedral: “To hell with Kerensky!”
q: On the almost deserted Nevsky, swept by a bitter wind, a crowd had gathered before the Kazan Cathedral, continuing the endless debate

present.size: a few workmen, some soldiers and the rest shop-keepers, clerks and the like

ref.q: a few workmen, some soldiers and the rest shop-keepers, clerks and the like

title: The Committee for Salvation outlawed
why: The evening after the rising was put down.
sum: At Smolny the Military Revolutionary Committee works without rest; new proclamations outlawing the Committee for Salvation litter the floor.
q: The Committee for Salvation had been outlawed.

title: The list of the dead
why: After Smolny (“Down-town again”); before Reed goes home in the small hours.
sum: Down-town again: the Duma is brilliantly lit and great crowds pour in. In the lower hall, amid wailing, the throng surges before a bulletin board listing yunkers killed in the day’s fighting; the telephone girls are testifying.
q: Down-town again. The Duma brilliantly illuminated and great crowds pouring in.

also.q: In the lower hall wailing and cries of grief; the throng surged back and forth before the bulletin board, where was posted a list of _yunkers_ killed in the day’s fighting
The telephone girls were testifying.

title: Lenin and the regiments
sum: Lenin addresses delegates of the city regiments, who vote to fight and elect a staff of five.
q: At ten in the evening Lenin addressed a meeting of delegates from the city regiments, who voted overwhelmingly to fight.

tp: in the small hours of the morning
title: The regiments march out
sum: In the small hours the regiments leave their barracks in full battle array; going home, Reed sees them pass through the deserted streets, swinging along with the regular tread of veterans, bayonets in perfect alignment.
q: Going home I saw them pass, swinging along with the regular tread of veterans, bayonets in perfect alignment, through the deserted streets of the conquered city

also.q: A Committee of five soldiers was elected to serve as General Staff, and in the small hours of the morning the regiments left their barracks in full battle array

ref.q: Going home I saw them pass, swinging along with the regular tread of veterans, bayonets in perfect alignment, through the deserted streets of the conquered city

title: “We are perfectly neutral”
why: The day session, before dusk.
sum: Mayor Schreider tells the Duma it is neutral, and that he kept the telephones to Smolny working while the yunkers held the Exchange.
q: We are perfectly neutral. When the Telephone Exchange was occupied by the yunkers Colonel Polkovnikov ordered the telephones to Smolny disconnected

ref.q: The city had again settled down to normal—shop-shutters up, lights shining

title: The battle of Pulkovo
sum: The MRC bulletin: by three in the afternoon the artillery fire reaches its height and the Cossacks are completely demoralised.
q: The artillery fire on the 12th of November developed with extraordinary force by 3 P.M.

tp: By this time it was dusk
title: The Committee for Salvation in hiding
sum: A friend takes Reed to apartment 229 at Nevsky 86, where the hunted Committee for Salvation is hiding; through the portières Reed glimpses Colonel Polkovnikov on the toilet, writing on a pad.
q: At Number 86 Nevsky we went through a passage into a courtyard, surrounded by tall apartment buildings.

also.q: a heavily-built officer in a colonel’s uniform sat on the toilet, writing something on a pad held in his lap.

ref.q: on the streets great crowds of people slowly moving up and down and arguing
There was a sound of scuffling; an inside door slammed; then the front door opened a crack and a woman’s face appeared.

title: “Falling back from Krasnoye Selo”
why: After dusk at Nevsky 86, by streetcar to Smolny.
sum: At the Petrograd Soviet Trotzky reports: the Cossacks fall back from Krasnoye Selo, heavy fighting at Pulkovo, and the Kremlin in the yunkers’ hands.
q: The Cossacks are falling back from Krasnoye Selo.

also.q: At Pulkovo heavy fighting is going on. All available forces must be hurried there

title: The Cossacks break
sum: Before midnight the Cossacks break and flee, leaving their artillery. The workers’ army rolls forward on a ragged front into Tsarskoye.
q: Before midnight of Monday the Cossacks broke and were fleeing, leaving their artillery behind them

title: Tsarskoye Selo retaken
sum: The MRC bulletin: by midnight Tsarskoye Selo and its wireless station are in Soviet hands, and the Cossacks retreat “towards Gatchina and Colpinno”.
q: By 11-12 P.M., Tsarkoye Selo, including the wireless station, was entirely occupied by the troops of the Soviets.
The Cossacks retreated towards Gatchina and Colpinno.

tp: almost three o’clock in the morning
title: “Kerensky is smashed!”
sum: Leaving the hall, Reed is met by Holtzman of the MRC, who reads out a pencilled telegram from the Pulkovo staff. It is dated in the Old Style.
q: It was almost three o’clock in the morning when, as we left the hall, Holtzman, of the Military Revolutionary Committee, came running down the hall with a transfigured face.

doc.q: Pulkovo. Staff. 2.10 A.M. The night of October 30th to 31st will go down in history.

title: A train for the sailors
why: Straight after the telegram, by car across Znamensky Square.
sum: At the Nicolai Station a member of the Vikzhel refuses to carry the massed sailors to Moscow, until a few railwaymen open another door: “This way, comrades!”
q: “This way, comrades!” cried one. “We will take you to Moscow—or Vladivostok, if you like! Long live the Revolution!”

also.q: All the seething Square roared at him; the sailors began to surge forward.

ref.q: Several thousand sailors were massed there, bristling with rifles.

title: Vera Slutskaya killed
why: The driver, that afternoon: “early this morning”.
sum: The driver points out the barren hill where the Bolshevik councillor Vera Slutskaya was killed by a shell from Kerensky’s armoured train “early this morning”.
q: here was where Vera Slutskaya died
It happened early this morning.

title: First snow
sum: Early in the morning, walking up to Smolny, Reed sees the first snow: “Good for the health!” says the soldier at the door.
q: Going up the long wooden sidewalk from the outer gate I saw the first thin, hesitating snow-flakes fluttering down from the grey, windless sky.

present.size: workers and soldiers, spattered and caked with mud

ref.q: Inside, the long, gloomy halls and bleak rooms seemed deserted. No one moved in all the enormous pile. A deep, uneasy sound came to my ears, and looking around, I noticed that everywhere on the floor, along the walls, men were sleeping.

title: Order Number I
sum: Muraviov’s order to the Pulkovo detachment: the enemy is routed and falling back on Pavlovsk II and Gatchina; advanced units hold the north-east edge of Tsarskoye Selo and Alexandrovskaya station.
q: November 13, 1917. 38 minutes past 9 a. m. After a cruel fight the troops of the Pulkovo detachment completely routed the counter-revolutionary forces
Our advanced units occupied the northeastern extremity of Tsarskoye Selo and the station Alexandrovskaya.

title: Volunteers at the ledgers
why: Between Smolny in the early morning and Smolny about noon.
sum: At the State Bank the new Commissar, Petrovitch, and sweating volunteer soldiers and sailors try to make sense of the ledgers the striking clerks left.
q: I went to the State Bank to see the new Commissar, a redhaired Ukrainean Bolshevik named Petrovitch.

title: An ambulance for the front
sum: About noon Reed gets a ride in a volunteer ambulance bound for the revolutionary front.
q: About noon I was again in front of Smolny, talking with the driver of an ambulance bound for the revolutionary front.

title: Lunch with the Engineers
why: After “about noon” at Smolny.
sum: The ambulance stops for lunch with the committee of the 6th Reserve Engineers’ Battalion in a barracks courtyard on the Kirochnaya.
q: On the Kirotchnaya we turned into an immense courtyard surrounded by military buildings

title: The road to the front
why: After lunch, on the way to Pulkovo.
sum: Down the Liteiny and the Zagorodny and under the Moskovsky Gate; the highway is thronged with Red Guards going out and coming back.
q: It was thronged with Red Guards, stumbling along on foot toward the revolutionary front, shouting and singing; and others, greyfaced and muddy, coming back.

also.q: Straight down the Liteiny we rattled, and along the Zagorodny Prospekt.

Passing under the huge grey stone archway of the Moskovsky Gate, covered with golden hieroglyphics, ponderous Imperial eagles and the names of Tsars, we sped out on the wide straight highway, grey with the first light fall of snow.

present.size: Red Guards, stumbling along on foot toward the revolutionary front

ref.q: It was thronged with Red Guards, stumbling along on foot toward the revolutionary front, shouting and singing

present.size: Women with spades, some with rifles and bandoleers

ref.q: Women with spades, some with rifles and bandoleers, others wearing the Red Cross on their arm-bands

present.size: Squads of soldiers marching out of step

ref.q: Squads of soldiers marching out of step, with an affectionate jeer for the Red Guards; sailors, grim-looking; children with bundles of food for their fathers and mothers; all these, coming and going, trudged through the whitened mud that covered the cobbles of the highway inches deep.

present.size: trucks bound both ways, bristling with armed men

ref.q: We passed cannon, jingling southward with their caissons; trucks bound both ways, bristling with armed men

Squads of soldiers marching out of step, with an affectionate jeer for the Red Guards; sailors, grim-looking; children with bundles of food for their fathers and mothers; all these, coming and going, trudged through the whitened mud that covered the cobbles of the highway inches deep.

present.size: others, greyfaced and muddy, coming back

ref.q: It was thronged with Red Guards, stumbling along on foot toward the revolutionary front, shouting and singing; and others, greyfaced and muddy, coming back.

title: The battlefield at Pulkovo
why: The ambulance’s first halt beyond the Moskovsky Gate.
sum: At Pulkovo, where the road divides and the ambulance halts, the crowds meet; houses at the cross-roads are pocked with bullets and the earth is trampled into mud.
q: A row of houses facing the cross-roads was marked with bullets, and the earth was trampled into mud half a mile around.

also.q: At Pulkovo the road divided, and there we halted in the midst of a great crowd

title: “I swung the axe”
why: After the stop at Pulkovo.
sum: Reed goes with the new commandant, Baklanov, to the commandant’s office in the Ekaterina Palace, and is handed an axe to break open the old commandant’s chest. It is empty.
q: I swung the axe. The wooden chest was empty.

also.q: The new Commandant of Tsarskoye Selo and I went toward the Ekaterina Palace

title: “They were going to shoot me!”
why: Before the “fast-deepening twilight” walk to the Rifles.
sum: At the first cross-roads on the road “toward Romanov” two illiterate soldiers take Reed off the truck for his odd pass and stand him against a wall.
q: led me to a wall, against which they placed me. It flashed upon me suddenly; they were going to shoot me!

also.q: The truck hurtled on toward Romanov, through the bright, empty day.
Down in front of the Soviet palace an auto-truck was going to the front.

title: Before the Regimental Committee
sum: At dusk the soldiers march Reed to the 2nd Tsarskoye Selo Rifles, whose committee overrules its colonel and votes to engage the Cossacks in the morning.
q: In the fast-deepening twilight we trudged along the muddy road.

also.q: It was dark when we came to the barracks of the Second Tsarskoye Selo Rifles

title: Dybenko goes to conquer Kerensky
why: After dark, back from the Rifles in their staff car.
sum: Back at the Soviet, Reed sees Dybenko climb alone into a car and drive off to Gatchina.
q: Alone, he climbed in the rear seat, and was off-off to Gatchina, to conquer Kerensky.

title: “My Petrograd!”
why: The night ride back from Tsarskoye.
sum: Riding back through the night in a truck of Red Guards without lights, Reed sees the capital from the heights; the old workman at the wheel cries, “All mine now!”
q: “Mine!” he cried, his face all alight. “All mine now! My Petrograd!”

also.q: I went back to Petrograd riding on the front seat of an auto truck, driven by a workman and filled with Red Guards.

title: Krasnov’s deposition
sum: General Krasnov’s statement: at three Kerensky summons him, accuses him of betrayal, and hears that his own Cossacks mean to hand him to the sailors.
q: To-day, about three o’clock (A. M.), I was summoned by the Supreme Commander (Kerensky).

title: Kerensky flees
why: Krasnov: “Half an hour later the Cossacks came to tell me that Kerensky was not in his quarters.”
sum: Half an hour later he is gone, alone, “disguised in the uniform of a sailor”. Reed gives no destination, and this map draws none.
q: And so Kerensky fled, alone, “disguised in the uniform of a sailor,” and by that act lost whatever popularity he had retained among the Russian masses

title: Krasnov surrenders
why: Reed gives no hour: after Dybenko reaches Gatchina on the evening of the 13th, and after the 3 A.M. summons in Krasnov’s deposition of the 14th.
sum: What Dybenko told the Cossacks “nobody knows”, but Krasnov, his staff and several thousand Cossacks surrender, and advise Kerensky to do the same. The Soviet appeal says Kerensky has fled.
q: General Krasnov and his staff and several thousand Cossacks surrendered, and advised Kerensky to do the same.

also.q: That chief of the counter-revolutionary campaign has fled.

title: The Kremlin surrenders
why: “That same day” as Lunatcharsky’s resignation, which Reed dates “On November 15th”.
sum: In Moscow the White Guards and yunkers in the Kremlin surrender and are allowed to march out; the Committee of Public Safety is dissolved.
q: That same day the White Guards and yunkers in the Kremlin surrendered, and were allowed to march out unharmed.

title: Trains “southwest” to Moscow
why: “For the past week”, written of the days before Reed’s own trip to Moscow.
sum: For a week the MRC and the railwaymen have held the Nicolai Railroad and sent train after train of sailors and Red Guards toward Moscow.
q: For the past week the Petrograd Military Revolutionary Committee, aided by the rank and file of the Railway Workers, had seized control of the Nicolai Railroad, and hurled trainload after trainload of sailors and Red Guards southwest

moves.size: trainload after trainload of sailors and Red Guards

present.size: trainload after trainload of sailors and Red Guards

ref.q: hurled trainload after trainload of sailors and Red Guards southwest

title: Red Guards march to welcome their brothers
