sum: Two thousand Red Guards march down the Zagorodny Prospekt behind a band playing the Marseillaise, to welcome home their brothers who had defended Red Petrograd.
q: On the evening of November 16th I watched two thousand Red Guards swing down the Zagorodny Prospekt behind a military band playing the Marseillaise

also.q: with blood-red flags over the dark ranks of workmen

ref.q: between silent crowds of bourgeois, contemptuous but fearful

I watched two thousand Red Guards swing down the Zagorodny Prospekt behind a military band playing the _Marseillaise_—and how appropriate it sounded—with blood-red flags over the dark ranks of workmen

title: The press decree crisis
why: “The night of November 17th”.
sum: At a packed and ominous Tsay-ee-kah, Bolsheviks attack the press decree; Lenin wins the vote, the Left SRs quit the Military Revolutionary Committee, and five Commissars resign.
q: On the night of November 17th the great hall was packed and ominous for the meeting of the Tsay-ee-kah.

title: “Uncle Tom’s Cabin”
why: An evening after the snow came; one Red Guard speaks of “last Sunday”, so probably the week after 11 Nov.
sum: One evening in a Red Guards’ traktir across from Smolny’s gates, an officer argues politics with the Red Guards at the tea tables.
q: I sat one evening in a traktir--a kind of lower-class inn--across the street from the gates of Smolny; a low-ceilinged, loud place called “Uncle Tom’s Cabin,” much frequented by Red Guards.

tp: About seven o’clock in the evening
title: The train to Moscow
why: Reed gives the hour, not the day. He decided to go once the Kremlin had been Bolshevik “for two days” (it surrendered on the 15th), and the Commissars who had just resigned were on the train: so the 17th at the earliest. The 19th is an estimate; Reed gives no date.
sum: About seven in the evening Reed’s train pulls out of the Nicolai Station, drawn by a weak wood-burning engine, with soldiers on the roof and debates in the corridors.
q: About seven o’clock in the evening we drew out of the station, an immense long train drawn by a weak little locomotive burning wood

present.size: a mob of shabby soldiers, all carrying huge sacks of eatables

ref.q: a mob of shabby soldiers, all carrying huge sacks of eatables, stormed the doors, smashed the windows, and poured into all the compartments, filling up the aisles and even climbing onto the roof

title: Rooms at the Hotel National
why: After a night and the next day on the train (“all night long”, then “until dark”): the evening after the departure.
sum: After a night and a day on the train and a sleigh down the shell-pocked Tverskaya, the Hotel National takes them in, as foreigners under the MRC’s protection.
q: At the big Hotel National they finally took us in; for we were foreigners, and the Military Revolutionary Committee had promised to protect the dwellings of foreigners....

title: Banners for the funeral
why: After dinner on the day of arrival; “Late in the evening” comes the Nobles’ Club.
sum: In the state salon of the Moscow Soviet half a hundred women sew red and black banners for the funeral; Rogov invites Reed to march with the Central Executive Committee next morning.
q: cutting and sewing streamers and banners for the Funeral of the Revolutionary Dead

also.q: He invited us to march with the Central Executive Committee in the funeral procession next morning

title: Nogin jeered at the Nobles’ Club
sum: The Moscow Bolsheviki meet in the Nobles’ Club theatre over the Commissars who resigned. The workers arrive about midnight, shout Nogin down, and cheer Bukharin.
q: Scarcely had the meeting formally opened before Nogin was assailed with a tempest of jeers and angry shouts.

also.q: Late in the evening I went to the Dvorianskoye Sobranie

title: Digging the Brotherhood Grave
why: After the Nobles’ Club meeting, which the workers reached “about midnight”; the night before the funeral.
sum: At night by the Kremlin wall, by firelight, hundreds dig two great pits for tomorrow’s burial.
q: “The Brotherhood Grave,” he explained. “To-morrow we shall bury here five hundred proletarians who died for the Revolution.”

also.q: Late in the night we went through the empty streets and under the Iberian Gate to the great Red Square

title: The funeral on Red Square
why: The morning after the arrival (Rogov invites them to march “next morning”); Reed gives no date. “All the long day”.
sum: All day the red-bannered procession enters Red Square by the Iberian Gate and leaves by the Nikolskaya while the coffins are lowered into the pits.
q: All the long day the funeral procession passed, coming in by the Iberian Gate and leaving the Square by way of the Nikolskaya

also.q: We rose before sunrise, and hurried through the dark streets to Skobeliev Square.
We set out down the Tverskaya, the banners flapping overhead.

title: The Peasants’ Congress opens
why: “By November 23d about four hundred had gathered”; the first session followed.
sum: The Extraordinary Peasants’ Congress meets in the Duma’s Alexander Hall: more than half Left SRs, a fifth Bolsheviki, a quarter conservative SRs.
q: The first session took place in the Alexander Hall of the Duma building

title: The peasants make terms
sum: After an all-night struggle in the secret conferences at Smolny, the Left SRs and the Bolsheviki agree: the Tsay-ee-kah is to be doubled by 108 members from the Peasants’ Congress, plus delegates of the Army, the Fleet and the Trade Unions.
q: Wednesday morning, November 28th, after a terrible all-night struggle, an agreement was reached.

also.q: a series of secret conferences were already going on between the Left Socialist Revolutionaries and the Bolsheviki at Smolny

title: Tchernov leaves the hall
why: The session at Fontanka 6 that Reed dates “on Wednesday afternoon”, after the morning’s agreement.
sum: At Fontanka 6 Tchernov goes between the Congress and the old Executive’s rump meeting; when he warns the Congress against the agreement, laughter drives him from the platform and the room.
q: He was interrupted by a great burst of laughter; and realising the situation, he left the platform and the room, taking his popularity with him....

title: A holiday feeling
sum: The Congress meets in extraordinary session in a holiday mood. Reed dates it “Thursday, November 16th”, an Old Style date (= 29 Nov), just after a New Style “November 28th”.
q: Late in the afternoon of Thursday, November 16th, the Congress met in extraordinary session.

also.q: There was a holiday feeling in the air; on every face was a smile
At the end Ustinov announced the arrival rival of a delegation from Smolny, accompanied by representatives of the Red Army, greeted with a rising ovation.

moves.size: a delegation from Smolny, accompanied by representatives of the Red Army

title: The torchlit march to Smolny
sum: Out of the building in the dark: the Pavlovsky Regiment’s band plays the Marseillaise, banners unfurl, and the peasants march with torches down the bank of the Fontanka to Smolny.
q: From somewhere torches appeared, blazing orange in the night, a thousand times reflected in the facets of the ice, streaming out smokily over the throng as it moved down the bank of the Fontanka singing

also.q: Along the bank of the canal were drawn up in full marching order the soldiers of the Pavlovsky Regiment, with their band, which broke into the Marseillaise.
So the great procession wound through the city, growing and unfurling ever new red banners lettered in gold.

say: Long live the union of the revolutionary and toiling masses!
We bow to this flag in order to create the brotherhood of all people!

present.size: the soldiers of the Pavlovsky Regiment

ref.q: Along the bank of the canal were drawn up in full marching order the soldiers of the Pavlovsky Regiment, with their band, which broke into the Marseillaise.

present.size: crowds that stood in astonished silence

ref.q: between crowds that stood in astonished silence

title: On the steps of Smolny
why: The procession’s arrival, after its march from Fontanka 6 (“So the great procession wound through the city”) and before the hall, where the Tsay-ee-kah “was waiting”: some 3.7 km at a procession’s pace from about half past six.
sum: Near Smolny the Red Guard lines both sides of the street. On the steps about a hundred Workers’ and Soldiers’ Deputies, massed with their banner, rush down to embrace the peasants, and the procession pours in through the great door.
q: On the steps of Smolny about a hundred Workers’ and Soldiers’ Deputies were massed, with their banner, dark against the blaze of light streaming out between the arches.

also.q: Near Smolny the Red Guard was lined up on both sides of the street, wild with delight.
Like a wave they rushed down, clasping the peasants in their arms and kissing them; and the procession poured in through the great door and up the stairs, with a noise like thunder

say: Long live the union of the revolutionary and toiling masses!
We bow to this flag in order to create the brotherhood of all people!

ref.q: Near Smolny the Red Guard was lined up on both sides of the street, wild with delight.

present.size: about a hundred Workers’ and Soldiers’ Deputies

say: Long live the union of the revolutionary and toiling masses!
We bow to this flag in order to create the brotherhood of all people!

ref.q: So the great procession wound through the city, growing and unfurling ever new red banners lettered in gold.

title: Two banners on one wall
why: On the procession’s arrival.
sum: In Smolny’s hall the two presidiums embrace, the two banners are hung together over the empty frame of the Tsar’s portrait, and the “triumphal session” opens.
q: behind them the two banners were intertwined against the white wall, over the empty frame from which the Tsar’s picture had been torn

title: The Duma turned out
why: Reed gives the date, not the hour.
sum: At the Duma’s meeting of 2 December an officer and sailors walk into the Nicolai Hall and order the members out; they go, “ceding to violence”.
q: At the meeting of December 2d, an officer and some sailors entered the Nicolai Hall while a member was speaking, and ordered the members to leave, or force would be used.
